claim_as_written: Recreational runners 3.5% OA prevalence; sedentary 10.2%; competitive 13.3%; n = 125,810
design: Systematic review and meta-analysis of observational studies (25 studies included, 17 meta-analysed)
population: Recreational and competitive runners vs non-running sedentary controls; hip and/or knee OA; n = 125,810 in review, 114,829 in meta-analysis
safe_wording: In a pooled analysis of 17 studies, 3.5% of recreational runners had hip or knee arthritis, compared with 10.2% of non-runners and 13.3% of competitive runners. The study could not tell whether running caused the difference.
notes: Figures match the abstract. Pooled prevalence only: the odds ratio for recreational runners vs controls was 0.86 (95% CI 0.69 to 1.07), not statistically significant; competitive 1.34 (0.97 to 1.86). Authors state causation could not be determined and previous injury may confound. Association only; never 'protective'. n = 125,810 is the review total; the meta-analysis used 114,829.

claim_as_written: Any ache up to 5/10 during or after exercise is a 'safe' signal
design: Silbernagel: RCT; Thomeé: RCT; Sandal: exercise cohort within an RCT
population: Silbernagel: 38 adults with Achilles tendinopathy; Thomeé: 40 young women with patellofemoral pain; Sandal: adults over 35 with knee or hip pain
safe_wording: A common clinical guide is that an ache during exercise is acceptable if it stays moderate (many clinicians use about 5 out of 10) and settles within 24 hours. This is clinical guidance, not a tested safety limit for arthritis. In one study of people with knee or hip pain, the small rise in pain after each session shrank over 8 weeks.
notes: Gilbert 2021 resolves (PMID 34948394, Gilbert SJ, Int J Mol Sci) but is a cartilage mechanobiology review; it contains no pain threshold. Do not cite Gilbert for this rule. The pain-monitoring model traces to Thomeé 1997 and Silbernagel 2007 (tendon and patellofemoral pain, not OA); neither abstract states the 5/10 number, so the number itself is unverified. Sandal 2015 (online; issue year may be 2016) shows exercise-induced pain flares shrink with sessions in knee/hip pain. PMID 26564575: do not cite until build confirms (year 2015 online vs 2016 issue unresolved in PubMed lookup). 'Safe' and 'does not signal joint damage' overstate: grade the number as clinical guidance. A2 decides final wording. Decision 2026-11-02 (Randy): keep as labelled clinical guidance, Unproven-Bridge, this safe wording; Gilbert 2021 stays rejected as its source.

claim_as_written: Chondrocytes convert mechanical strain into rebuild signals via the pericellular matrix
design: Narrative review of in vivo (animal, transgenic) and in vitro studies
population: Articular cartilage and chondrocytes; mostly animal and cell models
safe_wording: Lab and animal studies suggest that cartilage cells sense everyday joint loading through the material around them and use it to balance building and breakdown of cartilage.
notes: Citation swapped in source. Jiang 2021 resolves (PMID 33684550) but is about mitochondria and AMPK, not the pericellular matrix. The PCM claim is in Gilbert 2021 (PMID 34948394), which names aggrecan, type VI collagen, perlecan, decorin and biglycan exactly as the framework doc does. Use Gilbert 2021 for this claim. Mechanism in cells and animals, not shown in humans; 'rebuild' overstates (see C14). Decision 2026-11-02 (Randy): cited source changed to Gilbert 2021; PMID 34948394 re-read in PubMed on 2026-11-02 and its abstract states that PCM components transduce mechanical signals to chondrocytes and that physiological loading maintains the anabolic and catabolic balance.

claim_as_written: AMPK links mechanical force to mitochondrial health in chondrocytes; human dosing still emerging
source_as_cited: none given in course (framework doc, no citation)
design: Narrative reviews
population: Chondrocytes; preclinical evidence
safe_wording: Researchers have proposed that an energy sensor inside cartilage cells, called AMPK, may link joint loading to the health of the cell's mitochondria. This idea comes from lab research and has not been tested in people.
notes: Jiang 2021 abstract: 'We speculate that AMPK ... may play an important role in coupling force transmission to mitochondrial health.' It is a hypothesis. Alshorman 2026 review: evidence is primarily preclinical and the causal relationship remains to be established. 'Human dosing still emerging' understates it: there are no human dosing data. Copy must frame as hypothesis.

claim_as_written: OARSI and ESCEO rank structured exercise as Core Treatment, above NSAIDs and injections (and above opioids and acetaminophen)
design: Clinical practice guideline (expert consensus on GRADE-assessed meta-analyses)
population: Adults with knee, hip and polyarticular OA
safe_wording: International guidelines from OARSI (2019) list arthritis education and structured land-based exercise as core treatments for knee and hip osteoarthritis, recommended for essentially everyone with the condition.
notes: Bannuru 2019 = OARSI guideline. Core Treatments: knee = education + structured land-based exercise with or without dietary weight management; hip and polyarticular = education + land-based exercise. 'Above NSAIDs and injections' is a reasonable reading of core vs Level 1A/1B, but the guideline does not use the word 'above'; prefer 'core treatment for everyone' wording. ESCEO is a separate paper (Bruyere 2019, PMID 31126594); its abstract does not give tier wording, and ESCEO's algorithm differs from OARSI on some drugs, so do not name ESCEO in copy unless its full text is checked. Approved course framing (Randy, 2026-11-02): 'Exercise is medicine for the joint' rests on this row (OARSI core treatment, Established). It is a framing line, not a new claim; do not attach numbers or comparisons to it.

claim_as_written: Land-based exercise reduces knee OA pain by 12 points and improves function by 10 points on a 100-point scale; benefit lasts 2 to 6 months
design: Cochrane systematic review and meta-analysis of RCTs (54 studies)
population: Adults with knee OA; land-based therapeutic exercise vs no exercise
safe_wording: A Cochrane review of 54 trials found that land-based exercise reduced knee arthritis pain by about 12 points and improved function by about 10 points on a 0 to 100 scale right after treatment. Smaller benefits (about 6 points for pain and 3 for function) were still present 2 to 6 months later.
notes: 54 studies confirmed. Pain: 12 points (95% CI 10 to 15), 44 trials, high-quality evidence. Function: 10 points (8 to 13), 44 trials, moderate quality. Both are immediately post-treatment. At 2 to 6 months the effect shrinks to 6 points pain and 3 points function (12 studies). The source's 'benefit lasts 2 to 6 months' at 12/10 points overstates durability. Authors call the effect moderate, comparable with NSAIDs. Knee only. See C20 for the 'more durable and safer than medication' line.

claim_as_written: Cycling and aquatic exercise best for sharp pain; yoga for stiffness; resistance training for symptom control
design: Systematic review and network meta-analysis of RCTs (39 studies; SUCRA rankings); level of evidence 3
population: 2,646 adults with knee OA
safe_wording: In one network analysis of 39 trials in knee arthritis, all five exercise types studied helped. Cycling ranked highest for one pain score and walking distance, water exercise for another pain score, yoga for stiffness and daily function, and resistance training for overall symptoms. These rankings are options studied, not proof that one type is best for you.
notes: SUCRA rankings confirmed: cycling best for WOMAC-Pain (80.8%) and 6MWT (76.1%); yoga best for WOMAC-Stiffness (90.6%), WOMAC-Function, KOOS-ADL and KOOS-QoL; aquatic best for VAS pain (77.2%) and KOOS-Pain; resistance training best for KOOS-Symptoms (84.5%). Aquatic exercise was NOT significantly better than control on WOMAC-Pain. High risk of performance bias. Knee only, not hip. The course's 'sharp pain' is not an outcome in the paper. Write 'ranked highest in one analysis', never 'most effective'.

claim_as_written: After knee replacement, active resistance exercise beats conventional rehab on 6 of 9 measures; walking speed +0.13; TUG about 1 second faster; knee flexion +2.74 degrees; significant reduction in pain; active resistance is the evidence-based default
design: Systematic review and meta-analysis of RCTs (14 trials); GRADE certainty low
population: 880 adults after total knee arthroplasty; active resistance exercise vs conventional exercise (including CPM, home non-resistance exercise, body-weight exercise)
safe_wording: A review of 14 trials (880 people after knee replacement) found that lower-limb resistance exercise led to somewhat better walking speed, a slightly faster sit-stand-walk test (about 1 second), more leg strength and a little more knee bend (about 3 degrees) than standard exercise, measured right after the program. The overall quality of the evidence was low.
notes: 6 of 9 significant confirmed: max walking speed MD 0.13 (unit not stated in the paper text; likely m/s, do not print a unit), TUG -0.92 s, knee extension power SMD 0.58, flexion power SMD 0.38, ROM flexion +2.74 degrees, VAS MD -4.65 (scale not stated). Not significant: 6MWT, stair climb, ROM extension. Authors grade the evidence LOW and say effects are small, short-term only and 'may be beneficial' for mobility. Comparator is conventional exercise, not 'passive' rehab. 'Significant reduction in pain' and 'evidence-based default' overstate. Grade held at Promising despite RCT design because GRADE certainty is low; Decision 2026-11-02 (Randy): Promising confirmed.

claim_as_written: Strong quadriceps and hips act as shock absorbers and redistribute load off cartilage
design: Systematic review and meta-analysis of longitudinal cohort studies (11 studies); GRADE low
population: 46,819 adults without knee OA at baseline
safe_wording: People with weaker thigh muscles were more likely to develop knee arthritis over the following years, in studies of almost 47,000 adults. Whether stronger muscles protect the joint by absorbing load is still an idea, not a proven effect.
notes: Wei 2024 does not measure shock absorption or load distribution; it measures function, strength, ROM and pain after knee replacement. Citation does not support the claim. Re-sourced: Oiestad 2021 (online Dec 2021; journal issue 2022) shows quadriceps weakness associated with incident knee OA (OR 1.39 to 1.85), low-quality evidence. The shock-absorber / load-redistribution mechanism is Unproven-Bridge. Nothing found on hip muscles. PMID 34916210: do not cite until build confirms (year 2021 online vs 2022 issue unresolved in PubMed lookup).

claim_as_written: Fear-avoidance predicts disability more accurately than radiographic (X-ray/MRI) severity
design: Heuts: cross-sectional study; Holla: systematic review of 60 studies (qualitative synthesis)
population: Heuts: adults with hip or knee OA in primary care; Holla: knee and hip OA
safe_wording: In a study of people with arthritis, fear of movement was more closely linked with how well they managed daily activities than their X-ray findings were. Avoiding activity is also linked with weaker muscles and more difficulty with daily tasks.
notes: Heuts 2004: pain and pain-related fear (TSK) were significantly associated with functional limitations; radiological findings were not significant predictors. Cross-sectional, so 'linked with', not 'predicts'. Holla 2014: strong evidence in knee OA that activity avoidance is associated with activity limitations via muscle weakness; causal links unconfirmed. Holla 2015 (PMID 24905958, read): in a 5-year cohort, avoidance predicting later activity limitation lost significance after adjustment (P = 0.089). MRI was not studied: drop 'MRI'.

claim_as_written: Movers have 60% less arthritis than sitters
design: Derived from C01
population: As C01
safe_wording: In one pooled analysis, 3.5% of recreational runners had hip or knee arthritis, compared with 10.2% of non-runners. This is a link, not proof that running prevents arthritis.
notes: 60% is wrong: 3.5 vs 10.2 is about 66% lower in crude prevalence, and 'roughly a third' elsewhere in the source is the same ratio. But the adjusted odds ratio for recreational runners (0.86) was not statistically significant, so no relative-reduction figure should be stated. Also 'runners' is not 'movers' and 'non-runners' were defined as sedentary controls. Recommendation: drop the percentage reduction; print the two raw percentages with the C01 caveat. Decision 2026-11-02 (Randy): drop the 60% figure; raw 3.5% vs 10.2% only, as an association. Randy's message to keep: movement is good.

claim_as_written: Topical NSAIDs strongly recommended for knee OA; oral NSAIDs and injections second line; acetaminophen conditionally not recommended; opioids strongly recommended against
design: Clinical practice guideline
population: Adults with knee, hip and polyarticular OA
safe_wording: OARSI guidelines (2019) strongly recommend topical anti-inflammatory gels for knee arthritis, conditionally advise against acetaminophen (paracetamol), and strongly advise against opioids. Other medicines and joint injections depend on the joint and on your other health conditions, so talk them through with your doctor.
notes: Topical NSAIDs Level 1A (knee). Acetaminophen conditionally not recommended (Level 4A/4B). Oral and transdermal opioids strongly not recommended (Level 5). Corrections to the source table: intra-articular corticosteroid and hyaluronic acid are Level 1B/2 for KNEE only and NOT recommended for hip or polyarticular OA; oral NSAIDs depend on comorbidity (COX-2 Level 1B with GI comorbidity; no oral NSAID with cardiovascular comorbidity or frailty). ESCEO not verified (see C05). Medication copy is sensitive: Decision 2026-11-02 (Randy, clinical reviewer): approved; closing line changed to 'talk them through with your doctor' because medicines and joint injections are prescribed by a medical doctor. Name OARSI only.

claim_as_written: GLP-1 users who lose lean mass need resistance training and protein
design: Jobanputra: meta-analysis of RCTs; Villareal: RCT; Kim: systematic review and meta-analysis of RCTs
population: Jobanputra: adults on GLP-1 receptor agonists or SGLT2 inhibitors; Villareal: 160 obese adults 65 and over on a weight-loss program; Kim: adults over 50 losing weight
safe_wording: GLP-1 weight-loss medicines lead to some loss of lean (muscle) mass along with fat. In older adults losing weight by diet, resistance training and higher protein intake helped keep more lean mass. These studies were not done in GLP-1 users, so the benefit there is likely but not yet proven.
notes: Lean-mass loss on GLP-1 RA: MD -1.51 kg vs control; lean mass about 28% of weight lost (pooled with SGLT2i). Villareal 2017: lean mass fell 2-3% with resistance or combined training vs 5% with aerobic only, during diet-induced weight loss. Kim 2016: higher-protein diets retained more lean mass during weight loss in adults over 50. Direct GLP-1 + resistance + protein trials not found: applying these to GLP-1 users is Unproven-Bridge. Decision 2026-11-02 (Randy): include in first release, graded Promising.

claim_as_written: Rebuild cartilage / biological rebuilding / movement stimulates mechanotransduction to repair and maintain cartilage
design: Roos: RCT (4 months); Bricca 2018: systematic review of 9 RCTs (MRI cartilage); Bricca 2019: systematic review and meta-analysis of 12 RCTs (biomarkers)
population: Roos: 45 adults (30 analysed) at high risk of knee OA after partial meniscectomy; Bricca: adults with or at risk of knee OA
safe_wording: Exercise that loads the knee does not appear to harm cartilage in people with or at risk of knee arthritis. One small trial found signs of healthier cartilage content after 4 months of exercise. Exercise has not been shown to regrow lost cartilage.
notes: Bricca 2018 (MRI): mostly no effect on cartilage thickness, volume or defects; 'seems to not be harmful'; low quality. Bricca 2019 (biomarkers): exercise did not increase cartilage-turnover or inflammation markers; low quality. Roos 2005: GAG index improved vs control (dGEMRIC), small trial. 'Rebuild', 'repair' and 'regrow' are not supported in humans: grade Unproven-Bridge for those words; the 'not harmful' wording is Promising. Bricca 2018 was online 2018 but the journal issue is 2019; year in this row is the PubMed online year, PMID 29934429: do not cite until build confirms (year 2018 online vs 2019 issue unresolved in PubMed lookup). A2 bounds the wording.

claim_as_written: Immobilisation starves cartilage, tipping signalling toward a catabolic state within days
design: Hinterwimmer: prospective cohort with MRI; Vanwanseele: cross-sectional MRI comparison
population: Hinterwimmer: 20 adults on partial weight bearing for 7 weeks after ankle fracture; Vanwanseele: men with complete spinal cord injury vs healthy volunteers
safe_wording: When a leg is barely loaded for weeks, as after an ankle fracture, knee cartilage gets measurably thinner on MRI. Long-term loss of loading, as after spinal cord injury, is linked with steady thinning over months.
notes: Hinterwimmer 2004: 7 weeks partial load bearing gave 2.9% to 6.6% knee cartilage thinning. Vanwanseele 2002: 10% to 25% thinner at 6 to 24 months after injury. 'Within days' is not supported in humans (no human data found at that timescale): drop it. 'Starves' and 'catabolic signalling' are mechanistic framing (Unproven-Bridge); the measured outcome is thinning over weeks. Small samples, observational.

claim_as_written: Mitochondrial dysfunction in chondrocytes is a primary driver of OA pathogenesis
design: Narrative reviews (ex vivo human chondrocyte studies and preclinical data)
population: Chondrocytes from human OA cartilage and experimental models
safe_wording: Scientists have found signs of poorly working mitochondria (the cell's energy centres) in cartilage cells from arthritic joints, and they are studying whether this helps drive the disease.
notes: Blanco 2011: ex vivo studies report mitochondrial dysfunction in human OA chondrocytes, which 'may affect' pathways in cartilage degradation. Fernandez-Moreno 2022: argues OA 'could be considered' a mitochondrial disease. Neither shows it is a primary driver. 'Primary driver' overstates: never use.

claim_as_written: Tracker rule: if the joint feels worse 24 hours later, reduce your volume by 50% for the next session
design: None found
population: None
safe_wording: If your joint feels worse the next day, do less next time (for example, fewer repetitions or a shorter session) until it settles. This is clinical guidance, not a research-tested rule.
notes: No source found for a 50% reduction. Pain-monitoring studies (see C02) adjust load when pain does not settle by the next morning but no fixed percentage was found in the abstracts read. A2 decides whether the 50% figure stays, labelled as clinical guidance.

claim_as_written: Cartilage is like a sponge: if it stays dry and compressed it becomes brittle and breaks down; movement 'mechanically pumps' synovial fluid to feed it
source_as_cited: Gilbert 2021 (rejected; re-sourced 2026-11-02 to Mauck 2003 and Graham 2017)
design: Mauck: theoretical model checked against published experiments; Graham: ex vivo explant experiment; Zhang: theoretical model
population: Cartilage and cartilage-like gels; Graham used bovine knee osteochondral samples; no living human joints
safe_wording: Cartilage has no blood supply of its own. Its nutrients reach it mainly by moving in from the fluid inside the joint. Lab studies on cartilage samples suggest that joint movement and loading help move that fluid, and the larger molecules it carries, into the cartilage.
notes: Re-sourced 2026-11-02 at the coordinator's request. Avascular, nourished by diffusion: Zhang 2006 ('Diffusive transport must play an important role in transporting nutrients into cartilage due to its avascular nature') and Mauck 2003 ('A primary mechanism of solute transport in articular cartilage is believed to occur through passive diffusion across the articular surface'). Movement helps: Mauck 2003 says cyclical loading has been shown experimentally to enhance transport of LARGE solutes; Graham 2017 (bovine explants) found sliding articulation drove fluid and solute into the cartilage contact far beyond diffusion alone, and its abstract notes recovery is usually attributed to diffusion and mechanical 'pumping'. Limits: small nutrients such as glucose move mainly by diffusion; Gardiner 2007 (PMID 17671860, modelling, read) found dynamic loading had negligible long-term effect on IGF-I transport. No study in living human joints, so the 'movement helps' part stays Unproven-Bridge; the avascular part is standard anatomy. Gilbert 2021 stays rejected as a source. Zhang 2006 is not cached: online 2006, journal issue likely 2007; do not cite until build confirms. 'Brittle' dropped (decision 2026-11-02).

claim_as_written: Nutrition provides the substrates (protein, vitamin C) for matrix repair
design: Prospective cohort (Framingham)
population: 640 older adults with knee radiographs
safe_wording: In one long-running study, people who ate more vitamin C had less worsening of existing knee arthritis on X-ray. The authors called this preliminary. No study was found showing that protein intake repairs cartilage.
notes: McAlindon 1996: highest vs lowest vitamin C tertile OR 0.3 for OA progression; no association with incident OA; authors say findings 'warrant confirmation'. Promising at best for vitamin C, as an association. Protein for cartilage matrix repair: not found. 'Substrates for matrix repair' is biochemistry framing, not a tested human outcome. Decision 2026-11-02 (Randy): held, not for first release. Row kept for the record.

claim_as_written: Exercise improvements are often more durable and significantly safer than relying on long-term medication; fewer side effects than long-term medication
source_as_cited: Fransen 2015 (by placement, Lesson 2 script) and framework FAQ
design: Cochrane systematic review and meta-analysis of RCTs
population: Adults with knee OA
safe_wording: Exercise eases knee arthritis pain about as much as anti-inflammatory tablets do in trials, and serious side effects from exercise were not reported in these trials.
notes: Fransen 2015 says the effect is 'comparable with estimates reported for NSAIDs' and that no included study reported a serious adverse event (8 studies reported increased knee or back pain). It does not compare durability or safety against medication head to head. 'More durable' and 'significantly safer' are not supported as written. Decision 2026-11-02 (Randy): replacement wording approved. RETIRED by Randy 2026-11-02 (third follow-up): replaced by the framing line 'Exercise is medicine for the joint', which rests on C05 (OARSI core treatment, Established). Do not use this row's wording in copy. Grade left as it was.

claim_as_written: Movement is protective; for recreational doses, running is protective; sedentarism is a significant risk factor for OA
design: Systematic review and meta-analysis of observational studies
population: As C01
safe_wording: Recreational runners had lower rates of hip and knee arthritis than non-runners in this analysis. That is a link, not proof that running protects the joint.
notes: Causal wording ('protective', 'risk factor', 'Is running bad for my knees? No') must be recast as association (CLAUDE.md 7.4). Authors explicitly could not determine causation. See C01 and C11.

claim_as_written: Weight management is a core treatment for knee OA; weight management lowers systemic inflammation
source_as_cited: OARSI (by placement, framework doc sections 3 and 7)
design: Clinical practice guideline
population: Adults with knee OA
safe_wording: For knee arthritis, OARSI guidelines list weight management through diet, alongside exercise and education, as a core treatment for people who carry extra weight.
notes: OARSI 2019 Core Treatments for knee OA include structured land-based exercise 'with or without dietary weight management'; not listed as core for hip. The 'lowers systemic inflammation' part was not traced in this pass: do not use it without a source.

claim_as_written: Pain is a protective reflex: the brain's alarm goes off before any actual harm occurs; pain does not mean damage
design: Bedson: systematic search and summary of population studies; Bricca 2019: systematic review and meta-analysis of 12 RCTs; Fransen: Cochrane review of 54 RCTs
population: Adults with knee pain or knee OA
safe_wording: Pain is your body's alarm system. With arthritis, a moderate ache during exercise does not by itself mean the joint is being damaged.
notes: Sourced 2026-11-02 (third follow-up). Pain and joint structure often do not match: in population studies, 15% to 76% of people with knee pain had arthritis on X-ray, and 15% to 81% of people with X-ray arthritis had pain (Bedson 2008). Exercise did not raise blood markers of cartilage breakdown or inflammation (Bricca 2019, low-quality evidence). In the Cochrane review, the only adverse events reported were increased knee or back pain, with no serious adverse events (Fransen 2015). Two further sources agree but are not cached: Bricca 2018 (PMID 29934429, MRI: loading exercise does not appear to harm cartilage) and Sandal 2015 (PMID 26564575, exercise pain flares shrank over 8 weeks); do not cite these two until the build confirms their year. 'Alarm system' is an explanatory framing, not a measured finding. Not supported and must not be implied: that pain never signals harm, or that pain 'goes off before any actual harm occurs' as a rule. Sharp, worsening, swelling or not-settling pain stays a reason to stop and seek advice (A2 red flags).

claim_as_written: Structured sessions 2 to 3 times per week; individually delivered programmes work better
design: Cochrane systematic review and meta-analysis of RCTs
population: Adults with knee OA
safe_wording: In the Cochrane review, exercise programmes delivered one-to-one tended to reduce pain and improve function more than class-based or home programmes, though results varied a lot between studies.
notes: Fransen 2015 supports the delivery-mode point (with marked heterogeneity). The '2 to 3 times per week' frequency was not traced to a source in this pass; treat as clinical guidance until sourced.

claim_as_written: Exercise is often part of care for inflammatory arthritis (such as rheumatoid arthritis)
design: EULAR recommendations (consensus statement and practice guideline) informed by a systematic review and meta-analysis of 49 RCTs
population: Adults with rheumatoid arthritis, spondyloarthritis and hip or knee OA
safe_wording: European rheumatology recommendations (EULAR, 2018) advise that physical activity is part of standard care for people with inflammatory arthritis, such as rheumatoid arthritis, and for people with hip or knee osteoarthritis.
notes: EULAR 2018: 'Given the evidence for its effectiveness, feasibility and safety, PA is advocated as integral part of standard care throughout the course of these diseases' (rheumatoid arthritis, spondyloarthritis, hip/knee OA). The supporting meta-analysis (RMD Open 2018) found moderate gains in fitness (SMD 0.56) and strength (SMD 0.54) across these conditions. Covers physical activity and exercise; does not cover gout, lupus or other inflammatory conditions. Copy should not imply the course treats inflammatory arthritis.

claim_as_written: Osteoarthritis affects the whole joint, not just the cartilage
design: Narrative review (full text read)
population: Human OA joint tissues: cartilage, bone, synovium, menisci, ligaments, capsule
safe_wording: Osteoarthritis affects the whole joint, not just the cartilage. The bone under the cartilage, the joint lining, ligaments and, in the knee, the menisci can all change.
notes: Loeser 2012, 'Osteoarthritis: a disease of the joint as an organ' (no abstract in PubMed; full text read in PMC3366018): changes include cartilage degradation, subchondral bone thickening, osteophytes, variable synovial inflammation, degeneration of ligaments and menisci and capsule hypertrophy, and are 'the impetus for considering OA as a disease of the joint as an organ'. The paper also says OA 'is not simply a process of wear and tear'. Graded Established as a widely held expert definition backed by human pathology and imaging studies. Kraus 2015 (PMID 25865392, OARSI-linked definitions paper) was read but its abstract does not state the definition, so it is not used.

claim_as_written: Metabolic health is part of joint health
design: Courties 2017: narrative review; Baudart: meta-analysis of 48 observational studies; Kluzek: prospective national registry cohort; Louati: meta-analysis of 49 observational studies; Khor: systematic review and meta-analysis of 31 studies, BMI-adjusted where available
population: Adults with and without OA (knee, hip and hand); Kluzek: more than 75,000 Danish women with PCOS and matched controls
safe_wording: Joint health and metabolic health are linked. People with osteoarthritis more often also have high cholesterol, and the link shows up in the hands as well as the knees. Because hands do not carry body weight, researchers think whole-body factors such as low-grade inflammation may play a part, not just extra load. This is still being studied, and these studies show links, not proof that one causes the other.
notes: Sourced 2026-11-02. Dyslipidaemia: OR 1.98 overall, 2.27 knee OA, 2.12 hand OA (Baudart 2017; mostly cross-sectional, so association only). Weight-independent signal: in women with PCOS, hand OA incidence was raised (HR 1.8), and the knee and hand links remained after excluding women with obesity (Kluzek 2021). Courties 2017 review: in vivo models suggest metabolic diseases have a direct systemic effect on joints beyond weight (animal data: Unproven-Bridge for mechanism). Courties 2019 review (PMID 30584921, read; online 2018, issue likely 2019, NOT cached, do not cite until build confirms) states obesity is an established risk factor for OA at the hands as well as the knee. CONFLICT on diabetes: Louati 2015 found an unadjusted association (OR 1.46), but Khor 2020 found no increased OA risk with diabetes (OR 1.14, 0.98 to 1.33) and concluded body weight was probably the main confounder; prospective cohorts were null. Prediabetes also showed no independent link (Li 2022, PMID 35130571, read, not cached). Copy MUST NOT imply: that diabetes or blood sugar causes OA; that improving cholesterol, blood sugar or 'metabolism' treats, protects or reverses OA; that a 'metabolic OA' type is an established diagnosis; or any supplement or diet effect on joints. Safe framing only: linked, studied, not proven.
